# Statements

<a id="statements-nvs-is-the-only-open-tag"></a>

## `<?nvs` is the only code-mode open tag; `<?php` is refused

`rule:statements/nvs-is-the-only-open-tag`

`<?nvs` is the only code-mode open tag. The lexer still recognises `<?php` and switches to code mode on it,
purely so the parser can name the fix instead of misreading the rest of the file as inline HTML: the parser
reports `E0229` every time it consumes that token — at file start or at a mid-file reopen alike — and then
parses the code that follows normally, so nothing after the tag is swallowed.

```nvs
<?php echo 1; ?>          // tag rejected, `echo 1;` still parses as code
<?nvs echo 1; ?>          // unaffected
if ($x) { ?>html<?nvs }   // unaffected — reopening mid-block was always legal
```

`<?=` is untouched: it was never a spelling of `<?nvs`, it is sugar for `<?nvs echo`.

`<?php` and `<?nvs` always produced the same token past the parser, so the second tag preserved no
behaviour, only a spelling, and [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) rules out a second spelling
of one construct. Converting a file that opens with `<?php` is a five-character substitution with
nothing to analyse.

One file shape reaches code mode without a tag, and it is not a second spelling of one. A file whose first
two bytes are `#!` continues in code mode as if `<?nvs` stood there; writing the tag in a shebang file
before any `?>` is `E0009`.

**Declined:**
- **`<?php` as a permanent alias of `<?nvs`.** It differs in nothing, so it buys only a second thing to
  teach, the trade [`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast) and [`expressions/no-keyword-logical-operators`](expressions.md#expressions-no-keyword-logical-operators) also
  refuse.

<sub>See also [`statements/exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword`](statements.md#statements-exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword).</sub>

<a id="statements-one-namespace-statement-per-file"></a>

## `namespace X;` is the only namespace statement, once per file and before any declaration

`rule:statements/one-namespace-statement-per-file`

`namespace X;` is the only namespace statement, written once per file and before any declaration. The
braced form `namespace X { … }`, a second `namespace X;` in one file, and a `namespace X;` after a
declaration it would not cover are all `E0243` at parse time.

[`security/authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace`](security.md#security-authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace) keys authority on the namespace enclosing the code,
and [`config/an-application-is-its-entry-file-path`](config.md#config-an-application-is-its-entry-file-path) keys an application on its entry file. A file
that is two namespaces is a file whose authority depends on the line number, and neither rule has a
reading to give that. The rewrite is one file per namespace.

The braced form is still parsed after it is refused, so the declarations inside it report their own
problems in the same run.

<sub>See also [`security/authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace`](security.md#security-authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace), [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute"></a>

## A name containing a separator is read from the root, and one without it through the imports

`rule:statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`

Given a name as written, and the namespace and import set active where it was written:

- **Contains a separator** — it is the fully-qualified name, read from the root. The enclosing namespace
  and the import set are not consulted at all, **not even for its first segment**, which is what makes a
  namespace-prefix import (`use Core\Json;` then `Json\Derive`) name nothing.
- **Contains none** — look it up in the import set, then in the enclosing namespace, and nowhere else
  ([`statements/no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace`](statements.md#statements-no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace)).

A `use` therefore does exactly one thing: it binds **one declaration** under its own short name. Importing
a *namespace* is not a concept here.

```nvs
namespace App;

use App\Models;           // binds the name `Models`, and nothing under it
use App\Models\User;      // a `use` path was always absolute

new User();               // short: found in the imports
new App\Models\User();    // absolute — the same name from any namespace
new Models\User();        // refused: it names `Models\User`, which does not exist
```

`E0322` is the migration diagnostic, firing on exactly the construct this changes: *`Models\User` does not
exist; a qualified name is absolute here. Did you mean `App\Models\User`?* A short name for a class in the
same namespace, every `use` path, and `Core\Str::length($s)` are unaffected. A qualified name that
resolves neither way is the ordinary unresolved-name error.

The rule is decidable from the name alone, by whether it contains a separator, without knowing where the
name sits. PHP reads a qualified name relative to the current namespace, so inside `namespace App;` the
name `App\Models\User` means `App\App\Models\User`, and the error names a class nobody wrote. Here that
mistake cannot be written. The price is typing: reaching into a sub-namespace takes the full path or a
`use`, and a file wanting several names from one namespace writes one `use` per name.

**Declined:**
- **PHP's resolution kept as it is.** Two resolution rules and a token buy no meaning, and once a
  capability grant is keyed on a name's namespace ([`security/grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace`](security.md#security-grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace)),
  a name that resolves two ways is a grant that resolves two ways.
- **Relative qualified names kept, and only the leading separator removed.** It keeps the half where a
  name means different things in different namespaces, and removes the one way a reader could escape it.
- **A qualified name's first segment resolved through the imports.** It keeps the namespace-prefix import,
  at the cost of `App\Models\User` meaning one thing in a file that imports `App` and another in one that
  does not. `use Core\Json\Derive;` costs one line and reads as what it is.
- **The leading separator as the only way to write an absolute name.** It makes every `use` path and every
  `Core\Str` reference wrong, to reach a rule no easier to decide than this one.

<sub>See also [`statements/no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace`](statements.md#statements-no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace), [`statements/a-leading-separator-does-not-parse`](statements.md#statements-a-leading-separator-does-not-parse), [`statements/one-function-resolves-every-name`](statements.md#statements-one-function-resolves-every-name), [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name).</sub>

<a id="statements-no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace"></a>

## A short name resolves through the imports and then the enclosing namespace, and stops

`rule:statements/no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace`

A short name resolves through the imports and then the enclosing namespace, and stops. If neither has it,
the name does not resolve, and there is no third place to look.

A name declared at the root — a user class in the global namespace, or the reserved exception tree
(`Throwable`, `LogicError`, `TimeoutError` and their siblings) — is reached from inside a namespace by
importing it:

```nvs
namespace App;
use Throwable;

try { ... } catch (Throwable $e) { ... }
```

A single-segment `use` is not a special form; it is the ordinary absolute path to a name whose path happens
to be one segment long. The reserved tree gets no auto-import: a name that resolves without appearing
anywhere in the file is a name a reader cannot trace, and one closed roster's worth of exception is a
second resolution rule to hold alongside the first. Code at the root namespace is unaffected, because its
enclosing namespace *is* the root.

A root-namespace fallback only serves a function or constant call looking for a built-in from inside a
namespace. With no free functions and no free constants, nothing is left for one to do. The price is one
line: a namespaced file that catches `Throwable` writes `use Throwable;`, which PHP does not need.

**Declined:**
- **A fallback to the root for a short name that resolves nowhere else.** Two places could then match one
  short name, which is the ambiguity [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute) removes.
- **The reserved exception tree imported automatically.** A closed roster is still a second resolution
  rule, and `Core` gets no automatic import for the same reason ([`core-api/reserved-namespace`](core-api.md#core-api-reserved-namespace)).
- **The exception tree moved under `Core`, so that no root-level name exists.** It changes every `catch`
  clause to remove a case one import line already covers.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-leading-separator-does-not-parse"></a>

## A leading separator does not parse, in any of the three positions PHP writes one

`rule:statements/a-leading-separator-does-not-parse`

The leading separator is refused in all three positions a name could carry one, rather than stripped:

```nvs
\App\Models\User::find(1);   // refused
use \App\Models\User;        // refused
namespace \App;              // refused
```

`E0240` names the spelling without it: *a name is already absolute; write `App\Models\User` without the
leading `\`.*

Refusing rather than repairing is the reading ambiguous input gets everywhere: a spelling the compiler
silently accepts is a spelling that spreads. A qualified name is read from the root anyway
([`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute)), so the token has no work left to do, and accepting it
would restore exactly the two-spellings-one-meaning state removed here with the confusion moved from
resolution into style. The formatter does not strip it either — a construct the parser rejects never
reaches the formatter.

PHP gives the token two jobs and one ban, by position. In a `use` it is noise, because the path is already
absolute. Elsewhere it decides between two resolutions. In `namespace \App;` it is a parse error. A reader
moves between those three positions constantly, so no habit settles which one applies.

**Declined:**
- **Accept the leading separator and strip it, in the parser or the formatter.** That is the
  two-spellings-one-meaning state itself, moved into style.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute).</sub>

<a id="statements-one-function-resolves-every-name"></a>

## One function decides what a name means, and there is no second place that does

`rule:statements/one-function-resolves-every-name`

Name resolution is `nvs_hir::resolve_ref` and nowhere else. Every resolver in `nvs-hir` and `nvs-types`
already funnels through it — `extends` and `implements`, a `type` alias body, an attribute name, a static
call target, a `require` target, a route or command target — so the resolution rule is that one function's
body and none of its callers.

Keep it that way. A second place that decides what a name means is the state these rules exist to leave.
Because a capability grant is keyed on the namespace enclosing the code that asks, "which namespace does
this name sit in" is an authority question and not only a readability one: a resolution rule with two homes
is a grant lookup with two homes.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute), [`statements/no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace`](statements.md#statements-no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace).</sub>

<a id="statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name"></a>

## A declaration is reachable under exactly the name it was declared with

`rule:statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`

A class, interface, enum, method or constant is reachable under exactly the name it was declared with — its
own short name, or a fully-qualified path to it — and under no other.

`use Path\To\Name;` imports under the declared short name, full stop. Renaming an import is a diagnostic:
*imports cannot be renamed; refer to `Name` by its declared short name, or use the fully-qualified path
directly.* Nothing registers a second runtime-reachable name for a class either, and no such member is
coming later under another spelling.

The one real cost — two unrelated libraries choosing the same short class name — is paid at the call site
with the fully-qualified path: strictly more to type and strictly less to keep track of. Because no `as`
survives, making a bare `Str` resolve to an unrelated class is structurally unreachable rather than merely
refused, and the symbol table keeps exactly one entry per declared name, with no code path anywhere asking
whether a name was resolved directly or through an alias.

**One `use` names one import.** PHP's group form, `use App\Models\{User, Post};`, is `E0238` where the
`\{` is written, the sibling of the rename refusal on the other half of the same statement. The group
form does not give anything a second name, since every short name it introduces is still that name.
It is refused for simplicity: it is a second syntax for a statement that already exists, its payoff is
fewer lines, and its cost is that the short names a file introduces are no longer one per `^use` line
for a `grep`. The parser reports the brace group and skips it, so the statement still yields an import
for the prefix that was written and nothing downstream sees a half-parsed one.

**Declined:**
- **Import `as` kept for two libraries whose short names collide.** The fully-qualified name is more
  explicit for a little more typing, and a carve-out for collisions only does not stay narrow.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute), [`statements/no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace`](statements.md#statements-no-fallback-to-the-root-namespace).</sub>

<a id="statements-an-unused-use-is-a-warning"></a>

## A use line that no name reads is a warning, and its safe fix deletes the line

`rule:statements/an-unused-use-is-a-warning`

A `use` line that no name in its namespace scope reads is the warning `W1026`. `nvs check` reports it
for every file of the program outside a `vendor` directory, and the editor shows it on the open document
with the `Unnecessary` tag, which fades the line. It is the one entry an unused import gets: the editor
sends no separate dimming hint for it. An import whose path resolves to nothing has its own error and
no warning.

**A construct the language does not allow is always an error, and a warning is for code that runs as
written.** An unused import changes nothing a program does, so it never fails a compile, and `nvs run`
and `nvs serve` print nothing about it. Only `nvs check` and the editor report it.

The warning carries one safe edit that deletes the statement, and the whole line when nothing but blank
space or a `//` comment shares it, so `nvs check --fix` removes the line. A deprecated use that `--fix`
rewrites can leave an import unused, and the next pass of the same run deletes it. `nvs fmt` keeps the
line, since it is layout only and has no name resolution ([`tooling/fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic`](tooling.md#tooling-fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic)).

**The source is the editor's reference index.** A name reads an import when it is an identifier spelled
as the import's short name, in the same namespace scope, outside every `use` statement and not one
segment of a qualified name. `crates/nvs-lsp/src/index.rs`'s `reads` is that reading, the index keeps it
for organize imports, and `nvs_lsp::diagnostics::unused_uses` turns it into the warning for both
`nvs check` and the editor, so the two cannot disagree about a line. The reading errs one way only: a
method or a property spelled like the import counts as a read, so an unused import can go unreported,
and a needed one is never deleted.

What it costs is one more lexing of each file `nvs check` reads, and of the open document per analysis.
Nothing runs on the request path.

**Declined:**
- **The name resolution of `nvs-hir` as the source.** It would report every import a name resolves
  through, which is more exact, but a type annotation resolves in the type phase, so the warning would
  need a second record of reads across two phases. The editor's dimming would then read one source and
  `nvs check` another.
- **The warning on every compile.** `nvs run` and the test runner would print it beside the program's
  own output, and a case that freezes standard error would change with every unused import.

<sub>See also [`tooling/fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic`](tooling.md#tooling-fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic), [`tooling/fmt-sorts-the-use-block`](tooling.md#tooling-fmt-sorts-the-use-block), [`ide/no-refactoring-introduces-an-alias`](ide.md#ide-no-refactoring-introduces-an-alias), [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute).</sub>

<a id="statements-an-enum-name-is-a-type-everywhere"></a>

## An enum's name is an ordinary type, usable at every binding site a class name is

`rule:statements/an-enum-name-is-a-type-everywhere`

The `enum` keyword appears only at the *declaration*. Everywhere a type is used, an enum is spelled with
its own name, exactly like a class:

```nvs
enum Status { Active, Banned }

class Account {
    public Status $status = Status::Active;                // property
    public const Status DEFAULT_STATUS = Status::Active;   // class constant
    public static function ban(Status $s): Status { ... }  // parameter and return
}

Status $s = Status::Active;                                // local
foreach ($accounts as Status $status => $account) { ... }  // foreach binding
```

An enum name is an atom in the type grammar beside a class name — lexically identical to a class reference,
distinguished by what the name resolves to, the way `self`, `static` and `parent` are already contextual
there. Every binding site that requires a type takes one, with no position that admits a class name and
refuses an enum's.

An enum declared in a class or interface body ([`enums/class-scoped-enum`](enums.md#enums-class-scoped-enum)) is the same atom,
spelled `Owner::Status` anywhere and `Status` inside its owner, and its case is `Owner::Status::Active`.
Every binding site above takes the qualified form exactly as it takes the bare one:
`Account::Status $s = Account::Status::Active;` outside `Account` declares the same local that
`Status $s = Status::Active;` declares inside one of its methods.

<sub>See also [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct"></a>

## `require` is the only file-inclusion construct, and it runs every time it is reached

`rule:statements/require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct`

`require 'path.nvs';` is the only same-frame inclusion construct. It throws when the target is missing or
unparseable, and it executes every time control reaches it — there is no once-only guard.

```nvs
require 'partials/header.nvs';        // kept — throws if missing, runs every time
include 'partials/header.nvs';        // rejected
include_once 'lib/util.nvs';          // rejected
require_once 'lib/util.nvs';          // rejected
```

All four keep their token spellings in the lexer, so the diagnostic names the replacement precisely:
*Novis keeps exactly one inclusion construct; use `require` — it already throws on a missing file and runs
every time it is reached.*

**The path is known while compiling.** The file graph closes before the program runs
([`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload)), so `require` loads only a path the compiler can read. That
path is literal text (`'...'` or `"..."` with no interpolation), a class constant declared in a file
the walk has already read, or `.` between two of those. A relative path resolves from the file the
`require` is written in ([`programs/relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file`](programs.md#programs-relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file)). Every other path —
a variable, a call such as `Core\Path::thisDir() . '/autoload.nvs'`, an interpolation, a heredoc, an
`as` conversion, or a constant no file read so far declares — is `E0330` at the path, whose help
names `require './autoload.nvs';`. Such a site could load nothing and only ever throw. The one
`require` that still throws for a missing target at run time is a literal in a source with no
folder, such as standard input, which has no directory to resolve it from.

Throwing on failure is the failure path everything else takes ([`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation)); warn-and-continue
exists nowhere in the language. The repeat-guard axis is not needed either: declarations resolve by
namespace and through the per-path compiled-unit cache rather than by splice count, and a template partial
required from inside a loop must still run every time.

PHP spells one operation with four keywords across those two axes, which is the second name for one
behaviour [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) rules out. The survivor is `require` because its
PHP meaning is already exactly the kept behaviour, so a PHP file that writes it needs no rewrite. The
other three are refused for the behaviour each names, not for being PHP-shaped.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping `include` without its `_once` form.** Warn-and-continue is the one thing `include` adds over
  `require`, and its name would lead a PHP reader to expect it.
- **Keeping `require_once` beside `require`.** That is still two names on the repeat-guard axis, which
  has no work to do once declarations resolve by namespace.
- **A new, shorter keyword such as `load`.** Every PHP file that writes `require` would need rewriting
  for no change in behaviour.
- **A computed path that compiles and throws when it is reached.** No file is loaded for it while
  compiling, so it can never work, and the error belongs where the path is written.
- **An automatic once-guard as `require`'s only mode.** A template partial required in a loop would
  silently run once, trading one silent PHP behaviour for another.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals`](statements.md#statements-a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals), [`statements/a-require-expression-is-mixed`](statements.md#statements-a-require-expression-is-mixed), [`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals"></a>

## Declarations cross a `require` and variables do not

`rule:statements/a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals`

Every name a required file *declares* — a class, an interface, an enum, a `type` alias — is visible to the
requiring file exactly as if it had been pasted in. A local variable does not cross in either direction:
each file's top-level body is its own frame and is checked on its own, so a required file's `$x` is not the
caller's and the caller's is not the required file's.

The required file's own top-level statements run where the `require` is written, in source order, once per
time the site is reached — ordered against the statements around it rather than hoisted the way its
declarations are.

A required file never sees the includer's locals. A shared variable scope
would need one flow-sensitive definite-assignment analysis spanning a graph whose shape a `require` inside
an `if` decides at run time. A program that relied on it passes what it means as a constructor argument or
a static.

Nothing here is isolated: the required file runs in the caller's own process and request, with the
caller's capabilities. Isolation is what `spawn script` gives, and `require` gives none of it.

<sub>See also [`statements/require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct`](statements.md#statements-require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-require-expression-is-mixed"></a>

## A `require` used for its value hands back `mixed`, and converts like any other boundary

`rule:statements/a-require-expression-is-mixed`

`require` is an expression, and `$config = require 'config.nvs';` is its value form. The value is whatever
the target file's own file-scope `return` returned, or `1` when the file returns nothing at all, and it
cannot be known statically.

That is exactly the case `mixed` exists for, so the value needs the same explicit `as` conversion any other
boundary value of unknown-until-runtime shape needs before it can populate a typed binding. No special case
is carved into the type system for `require`, and nothing about the construct is a second unchecked
position.

<sub>See also [`statements/require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct`](statements.md#statements-require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct).</sub>

<a id="statements-static-is-a-member-modifier"></a>

## `static` marks a class member and names a class-relative type, and nothing else

`rule:statements/static-is-a-member-modifier`

`static` is a class-member modifier and a class-relative type. Static methods, `static::`, `new
static()` and `: static` all bind late, to the called class, and `new static()` compiled as `new
self()` would return the wrong class rather than fail to compile. A static method called through an
instance, `$base->m()`, names the object's run-time class, as `$this->m()` does: a `Child` held in a
`Base` variable runs `Child::m`, which reads `Child` as `static`. A callable taken with `static::m`
keeps the frame's called class and runs that class's `m`. A static property does not:
its storage is fixed where the access is written, so `static::$prop` is refused (`E0499`). For a
subclass that redeclares the property it would silently name the parent's storage, while a reader
expects the called class's. `self::$prop` and a written class name say which storage is meant.
A static property is never reached through an instance: `$p->x` and `$p?->x` are `E0869`, whose
message names `P::$x`, because an instance has no slot for it.
`static::class` is the called class's own name,
read at run time off the descriptor the frame already holds.

A `static` anywhere in a parameter type or a return type is the class the call names, at
`Category::find(...)` and at `$category->find(...)` alike: `property<static>`, `array<static>`,
`?static` and `: static` are all bound at the call. A base class that declares
`sortBy(property<static> $field)` once then checks each subclass's own properties at each call, with
no override per subclass. A type that also writes `self` or the declaring class's own name is not
bound, and neither is a `static` among a written callable's parameters; both keep the declaring class.
Inside the body the checker does not know which subclass called it, so a `property<static>` is the
property's name as a `string`, which the body may print, compare or convert back with `as
property<self>`, checked at run time. A key of `static` read on `$this` would be sound, but the body
types `$this` as the declaring class and cannot tell it from any other value of that class.
A `propertyPath<static>` is the path's text in the same way, and a `string<…static…>` is a `string`.
To reach `Core\Str::parts` or `Core\Reflect::steps` ([`core-classes/str-parts-and-reflect-steps`](core-classes.md#core-classes-str-parts-and-reflect-steps))
the body converts the text with `as propertyPath<self>` or `as string<propertyPath<self>>`, checked
at run time against the declaring class. A path through a property only a subclass declares throws
there: `steps` reads the class a path starts at off the argument's type, and the body has no type
naming the subclass.

`static::NAME` is late-bound the same way, and it is the one class-constant read that is not inlined:
the frame's called class is asked for `NAME` when the read runs, so a default method or an inherited
body reads the implementor's override where `self::NAME` reads the declaring class's value. Three things
follow from that read being a run-time one. A redeclaration of an inherited constant keeps a type
assignable to the ancestor's, in every class and interface, because the read is typed where the
constant is declared and answers whichever class the call was made on (`E0833`). The read converts
the called class's value to that type: a subclass's `int` read where `int|string` is declared is that
union holding the `int`. Nothing converts an `int` to a `float` there, so `int` over `float` is
`E0833` too, as it is for an override's return type. A `static::` constant
is refused in a constant expression — a default, a payload — which is folded once with no call to bind
it to (`E0831`). A `static::` read of a constant with no scalar value — an `array`, an object, `null`
— is refused, because the called class's table carries `string`, `int`, `uint`, `bool` and `float`
and nothing else (`E0832`); `self::` and the class name still inline such a constant.

An anonymous function's body is a frame of its own and carries no called class, so `static::` in any
form inside one is refused (`E0834`). `self::m()` and `parent::m()` inside one call the class the
anonymous function is written in,
as a written class name would: a static method reached that way reads that class as `static`, whichever
subclass the enclosing method was called on. An instance method reached that way is called on the
anonymous function's `$this`, which the call captures, and reads `$this`'s class as `static` as it
does everywhere. For `parent::m()` the class the call is made on is still the one the function is
written in: the parent is only where the method is looked up. PHP forwards the enclosing method's
called class into the anonymous function instead, so there a static method reached this way sees the
subclass. `self::` already means the written class for constants, `::class` and `self::m`, and
this reading stores nothing new.

A site that sets the called class leaves no late binding to reach an override, so a call from one to an
`abstract static` method is refused where it is written (`E0835`) unless the class it names, or a class
or interface above it, declares the method with a body. That is `Page::title()` on the abstract class
that declares `title`, and `self::title()` inside an anonymous function in `Page`'s methods. `self::`, `static::` and
`parent::` in a method body forward the called class and are not refused, so an inherited static method
calling `self::title()` runs the subclass's body.

A `static` member declares its type like every other member — `public static int $n = 0;` — and a body
declaring `static`, `?static` or `array<static>` as its return type may not return the declaring
class, since a subclass call site is promised its own (`E0741`). What it may return is `$this`, `new
static(...)`, `null`, a call on `static::`, `self::`, `parent::` or `$this` whose own return binds
`static`, a `? :` of two of these, or an array literal of them. A local variable is none of these, so
an `array<static>` built up in a loop is refused, and declaring `array<self>` is the way to write it.

The keyword therefore has one meaning per position: a modifier before a member, a type or a scope in an
expression. Nothing about it depends on whether it appears inside a function body, because inside a
function body it is not a declaration at all — see [`statements/no-function-static-and-no-global`](statements.md#statements-no-function-static-and-no-global).

Late static binding stays because fluent builders, record-style models and static factories are
written with it.

- **Memory:** only code that writes `static::` on a constant pays for the late read. Each read scans
  the called class's constant table, which is the size its declarations wrote, and builds the name as
  a fresh string released when the read returns. A `string` constant costs one allocation per read,
  charged to the isolate, as `static::class` does: the process-wide table's strings are not shared
  across isolates. `self::NAME` and `Class::NAME` still inline and cost nothing at run time. A
  `self::m()` or `parent::m()` call inside an anonymous function sets a class fixed at the call site
  and costs nothing, and only one that reaches an instance method captures `$this`. Binding `static`
  in a parameter or a return is the checker's, once per call it resolves, and costs nothing at run time.

**Declined:**
- **Refusing `static::NAME`.** It would be sound, but it drops a meaning PHP programs rely on: a
  default method that reads the implementor's constant.
- **Choosing the constant per called class at compile time.** The checker does not hold the set of
  classes a body can be called on, since a class in an autoload root nobody has named yet is still a
  caller.
- **Reading an `array` constant late.** The table stores a folded scalar, so an array would have to be
  rebuilt from its constant form on every read, a second constant builder beside the compiler's.
  `self::` still inlines it.
- **Carrying the enclosing method's called class into an anonymous function.** It is PHP's meaning
  and would admit `static::` there too, but the function object has no slot that holds a class, so it
  is a change to the layout of every anonymous function. It is the better answer if that slot is ever
  added.
- **Refusing `self::m()` and `parent::m()` inside an anonymous function, as `static::` is.** Every
  anonymous function that calls a private static helper would have to name its class in full.
- **Writing the class into each subclass's override of a method taking `property<static>`.** It is the
  boilerplate late binding exists to remove, and a missed override checks against the base class's
  properties.
- **Binding `static` in a parameter at run time.** The call site already names the class, so the check
  belongs where the call is written.
- **A `static` type kept apart from the declaring class inside the body.** It would let a body read a
  `property<static>` on `$this`, and every consumer of a type would have to learn a second meaning of
  a class. The body's `string` and `E0741`'s list cover the programs that need it.
- **Dropping late static binding along with the storage meanings.** `new static()` compiled as `new
  self()` returns the wrong class, and no annotation a program could add keeps the original behaviour.

<sub>See also [`statements/no-function-static-and-no-global`](statements.md#statements-no-function-static-and-no-global), [`statements/an-anonymous-function-captures-this-only-where-it-uses-it`](statements.md#statements-an-anonymous-function-captures-this-only-where-it-uses-it), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-no-function-static-and-no-global"></a>

## A function holds no state of its own, and `global` does not exist

`rule:statements/no-function-static-and-no-global`

Two spellings are refused, and each diagnostic names its replacement:

- `static int $calls = 0;` in a function — *function-scope `static` is not supported; declare a
  `private static` property on a class, or pass the value as a parameter*.
- `global $x;` — *`global` is not supported; pass `$x` as a parameter, or make it a `static` property or a
  `const`*.

A diagnostic that says only "not supported" is a bug against this rule, not a faithful implementation of
it.

A function static is the one binding whose definite assignment cannot be checked: its initialiser runs on
the first call and on no later one, so on every call after the first the binding is live while its
initialiser is not on the executed path. It is also a third storage class for one keyword — a per-function
slot, per isolate, with a run-once flag the JIT cannot fold away — and it hides from the signature that a
function's result depends on how often it has been called. A function static could never outlive its
request in any case, so nothing a program could rely on across requests is lost.

Without it, an isolate has one table of statics, the class statics, with one lifetime and one teardown
path, so a fresh isolate is fresh by building that one table again. Every use of a function static has a
better-placed replacement with a name, a type, a visibility and a home: a cache is a `private static
array<T>` on the class that owns it, where it can also be cleared and inspected; a one-time
initialisation is a static property or a constant; a call counter is a static property. The rewrite is
not always local: a free function in a procedural file needs a class to hang the property on, or a
parameter to carry the state.

`global` hides a function's inputs from its signature in the same way, and a `const` already covers
everything a read-only global would be used for.

**Declined:**
- **A function static with a type slot.** It would put the one exception into the definite-assignment
  analysis that the mandatory annotations pay for ([`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration)).
- **A function static whose initialiser runs when the isolate starts.** A side-effecting initialiser
  would run at a different time than the code says, and the second table of statics would remain.
- **`global` for reading only.** The function's inputs are still missing from its signature, and a
  `const` reaches every read-only value the declared way.
- **A `#[Memoize]` attribute as the replacement for a cache.** A caching construct has questions of
  its own (how a key is derived, how long an entry lives, how large the cache may grow), and it is a
  feature with its own rule if it ever exists, not part of this one.

<sub>See also [`statements/static-is-a-member-modifier`](statements.md#statements-static-is-a-member-modifier), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call"></a>

## A program holds state in five declared places, and the list is closed

`rule:statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`

Exhaustive by construction. A design that needs a slot not on this list changes this rule; it is not an
implementation detail:

| storage | lifetime | declared |
|---|---|---|
| local variable, parameter | the call | `int $n = 0;` |
| class static property | the isolate | `private static int $calls = 0;` |
| class constant | the isolate, immutable | `public const int MAX = 10;` |
| object property | the object | `public readonly uint $id;` |
| top-level script variable | the script's own frame, unreachable from a function | `int $n = 0;` at file scope |

There is no global constant: a constant is never declared outside a class, so "class constant, global
constant" is one row rather than two, and the free-floating half has nothing left to name. There is no
superglobal row either — host-populated request, session and CLI state is the class-static row, filled by
the host at isolate construction instead of by a user initialiser
([`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables)). An enum case needs no row: it is a compile-time constant
of its enum's integer type, inlined at every use site like any other literal.

**A class static belongs to the request, never to the process.** Each declared static has one slot per
in-flight request, set from the declaration's own initializer when the request's context is built and
released when it ends. A process-global static is a channel from one request into the next: a token
cached in one is readable by whoever sends the next request, and no care in user code closes that, so
security and request isolation settles it. `nvs run` cannot tell the two apart, because a CLI run is
one request, and `nvs serve` is where the difference shows. What it costs is PHP's process-lifetime
memo, which [`security/isolate-shares-nothing`](security.md#security-isolate-shares-nothing) already removes. A cache that must outlive a
request is a `Core` capability with a stated lifetime, not a class variable. A static has no
constructor to assign it, so its declaration carries an initializer unless its type admits `null`
(`E0409`), and a nullable one starts each request at `null`.

- **Memory:** one slot per declared static per in-flight request, released with the request, so the
  total is O(in-flight) and never grows with requests served.

The last row is the one to read twice. A top-level `$x` in a `.nvs` file is a local of the script's own
frame and nothing more. The script body is a function, so its variables are locals, and with no
`global` no other function can see them ([`statements/no-function-static-and-no-global`](statements.md#statements-no-function-static-and-no-global)). The
shared-nothing story holds at file scope for the same reason it holds everywhere else.

<sub>See also [`statements/no-function-static-and-no-global`](statements.md#statements-no-function-static-and-no-global), [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables), [`statements/a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals`](statements.md#statements-a-required-file-shares-declarations-not-locals).</sub>

<a id="statements-an-isolate-has-its-own-statics"></a>

## An isolate's class statics are its own, and a child cannot reach its parent's

`rule:statements/an-isolate-has-its-own-statics`

An isolate's context is built with a **statics base of its own**, and that single word is the whole of "a
child cannot read or write a parent static". Globals, class statics and runtime-defined constants are fresh
per isolate.

Compiled code loads a static inline through that base, so the same compiled function reads a different
store depending only on which context it runs under — which is why sharing compiled code between isolates
costs nothing and needs no per-isolate compilation.

A task is the other construction, and deliberately not the same one: a task shares the request, so it
aliases the request's static-property base rather than freshening it, and a child with a store of its own
would give one request two copies of every static. Collapsing both into one helper with a flag would leave
the next field added to the context classified by whoever adds it rather than by whoever needs it fresh.

<sub>See also [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call), [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables).</sub>

<a id="statements-no-host-populated-variables"></a>

## No variable is ever populated by the host; every superglobal is a `Core` class member

`rule:statements/no-host-populated-variables`

No variable is ever populated by the host. Every fact PHP hands a script through a superglobal is returned
by a `static` method on a reserved `Core` class, populated per isolate:

| PHP | replacement |
|---|---|
| `$_SERVER` | `Core\Server` — server metadata and request headers |
| `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_COOKIE`, `$_FILES` | `Core\Request` — query, body, cookie and upload input |
| `$_SESSION` | `Core\Session`, after an explicit `Core\Session::start()`; there is no auto-start |
| `$_ENV`, `getenv()` | `Core\Env` |
| `$argv`, `$argc` | `Core\Cli` — the CLI entry point only |
| `$_ARGS` | `Core\Script::args()` |

`Core\Server` and `Core\Request` are two classes rather than one, matching the split between facts about
the server and input the client sent. The value handed back keeps the shape any other boundary value has —
structured input as `array<mixed>`, a scalar payload not yet asserted to be text as `bytes` — so it needs
an explicit `as` before it populates a typed binding.

Each rejected spelling is diagnosed by name and names the `Core` class that replaces it.

A superglobal is untrusted input with no declared boundary: it is simply present, readable and writable
from any scope. A method call on a named class is a declared, traceable entry point, so a reviewer sees
which class, and therefore which trust boundary, each line depends on. With this rule a script learns
anything from outside itself in one way only — a declared class member, an object property or a
parameter — the same answer [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call) gives for state.

**Declined:**
- **The superglobals kept as read-only variables.** A read-only bare variable is still not imported
  or declared anywhere, and it fits no row of [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).
- **One class for every request and server fact.** One class for unrelated concerns is a global
  namespace with extra syntax ([`classes/no-free-functions-or-constants`](classes.md#classes-no-free-functions-or-constants)).

<sub>See also [`statements/globals-and-request-are-dropped-outright`](statements.md#statements-globals-and-request-are-dropped-outright), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call), [`errors/cookie-name-bytes`](errors.md#errors-cookie-name-bytes).</sub>

<a id="statements-globals-and-request-are-dropped-outright"></a>

## `$GLOBALS` and `$_REQUEST` have no replacement of any kind

`rule:statements/globals-and-request-are-dropped-outright`

`$GLOBALS` and `$_REQUEST` are dropped with no replacement of any kind: no `Core` class, no method, no
later addition under a different name.

`$GLOBALS` is not data the host hands a script — it is a reflective view onto the script's *own* variable
table, keyed by name and mutable in both directions. A top-level variable is a local of the script's own
frame ([`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call)), so there is nothing left for it to expose that a
`static` property, a constant, an object property or a parameter does not already reach the declared way. A
replacement would have to enumerate a frame's locals reflectively, which nothing else here does, or become
a second informally-scoped static bag.

`$_REQUEST`'s only job is merging three sources whose read-site names — `Core\Request::query()`, `::post()`
and `::cookie()` — already say which one a value came from. A merged accessor would either fix an order,
re-deriving the `request_order` footgun, or take the order as an argument, at which point it is no shorter
than naming the source.

<sub>See also [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables), [`statements/storage-that-outlives-a-call`](statements.md#statements-storage-that-outlives-a-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-an-anonymous-function-captures-this-only-where-it-uses-it"></a>

## An anonymous function captures `$this` only when its body names it, so `static fn` has nothing left to assert

`rule:statements/an-anonymous-function-captures-this-only-where-it-uses-it`

An anonymous function captures `$this` only when its body uses it, decided by the compiler.
`static function () {}` and `static fn() => …` are refused with `E0210`, which says that `static` is
not a modifier an anonymous function takes and that the keyword can simply be dropped.

`static fn` is an **assertion** that an anonymous function does not capture `$this`, and there is no
assertion syntax here — everything else in the language is a declaration the compiler enforces. The
property it asserted is obtained by making it true instead.

The effect is the one the keyword existed to produce: a callable that never mentions `$this` cannot
extend the enclosing object's lifetime. The cost is the corner — a `$this`-free anonymous function
built inside a method and then bound to a *different* object gives a callable that ignores the
binding, because `bindTo()` and `bind()` return an equivalent callable rather than rebinding anything.

<sub>See also [`statements/static-is-a-member-modifier`](statements.md#statements-static-is-a-member-modifier).</sub>

<a id="statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling"></a>

## A by-reference binding is written `inout`, in the modifier slot before the type

`rule:statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`

`inout` is a reserved word, written **before the type**, in every position a by-reference binding is legal:

```nvs
public static function bump(inout int $slot): int { … }

foreach ($xs as inout int $v) { … }
[inout int $a, inout int $b] = $pair;
```

It sits in the modifier slot the parser already reads ahead of the type, so `inout int $x` reads like the
`public readonly int $x` beside it and costs the grammar nothing.

The word names the mechanism. A parameter is copy-in/copy-back through a cell the call stages: the callee
gets the cell's address, and the value is copied back after the call returns — a callee that throws is the
one path that does not reach the write-back, so a caller sees no partial write. A `foreach` value binding
is the other mechanism, pushing each assignment through to the array element as it happens. Neither is an
alias.

**An `inout` parameter belongs only to a frame the call site outlives.** The copy-back is sound because
the callee's frame ends before the site's does, and two declarations break that order, so both are
refused where they are written. Calling a **generator** runs none of its body: it allocates the state
object and returns ([`iteration/generators`](iteration.md#iteration-generators)), so the staged cell is gone before the first
`advance()` while the parked frame would still address it (`E0492`). An **anonymous function** has no
call site that could stage anything: its by-value capture ([`types/implicit-capture`](types.md#types-implicit-capture)) lets it
outlive every frame in scope where it was written, so there is no frame whose end the copy-back could
be ordered against (`E0493`). A written `callable` signature ([`types/callable-signature`](types.md#types-callable-signature)) gives a
site a parameter list to read and still no call site at which to stage a cell. Neither is a lowering
left unwritten: copying the value in would stop being a reference, which is the observable point of
`inout`. Shared mutable state is an ordinary object captured by value, and a generator takes the value
and `yield`s what its body computes from it.

An anonymous function **capturing** an enclosing `inout` parameter is a different question and is
allowed: capture is by value, so the function holds a snapshot of the cell's value taken where it is
written, and can outlive the call that staged the cell.

Languages split on this word by mechanism. Those that alias write `ref`, `&` or `var`; those that copy in
and copy back write `inout`, as Hack and Swift do. Novis copies, so it takes the second word.

**Declined:**
- **`ref`.** In the languages that spell it so, `ref` is a true alias, and Novis has no alias: `$a = &$b`
  is refused because there is nowhere to put a reference. The word describes neither of the two mechanisms
  above.
- **`&` kept at the declaration.** It is one of `&`'s five meanings, and it names the aliasing PHP does
  and Novis does not ([`statements/ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker`](statements.md#statements-ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker)).

<sub>See also [`statements/inout-is-written-at-the-call`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-written-at-the-call), [`statements/ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker`](statements.md#statements-ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker), [`statements/an-inout-argument-is-a-local`](statements.md#statements-an-inout-argument-is-a-local).</sub>

<a id="statements-inout-is-written-at-the-call"></a>

## An argument that binds an `inout` parameter says so at the call

`rule:statements/inout-is-written-at-the-call`

An argument bound to an `inout` parameter carries `inout` at the call, and an argument bound to a by-value
parameter must not:

```nvs
int $n = 5;
echo Adder::bump(inout $n), " ", $n, "\n";   // "6 6"
```

This is not inference-assisted and it is not optional. A marker the compiler fills in silently is the
invisible mutation the rule exists to remove; it would make the requirement a style rule rather than a
rule, and a program that omitted it everywhere would still compile and still hide the write. Two mistakes,
two diagnostics: `E0713` is an argument that binds an `inout` parameter without saying so, `E0714` one that
says so where nothing binds it — including a call through a `callable`.

`foreach` and destructuring have no call site, so for them the declaration spelling
([`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling)) is the whole of it.

Without the marker, `Adder::bump($n)` and `Adder::sum($a, $b)` look the same at the call, and only one of
them writes its argument. Somebody reviewing code they did not write has to see that write where it
happens, so an invisible mutation is a security question and not a matter of taste. The price is typing:
`bump(inout $n)` is longer than `bump($n)`, and it says what `bump($n)` did not.

**Declined:**
- **`&` at the call site, beside `&` at the declaration.** `f(&$x)` reads as an address-of or a bitwise
  AND, and `&` keeps every one of its meanings ([`statements/ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker`](statements.md#statements-ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker)).
  PHP removed call-time `&` for exactly that confusion.
- **The declaration renamed, with no marker at the call.** It spends a breaking change on the name and
  leaves the mutation invisible, which is the larger of the two problems.
- **The marker inferred at the call, with a warning where it is missing.** That is the compiler filling it
  in, which the paragraph above already rules out.

<sub>See also [`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling), [`statements/an-inout-argument-is-a-local`](statements.md#statements-an-inout-argument-is-a-local).</sub>

<a id="statements-an-inout-argument-is-a-local"></a>

## An `inout` argument is a local or an instance property, and never an element

`rule:statements/an-inout-argument-is-a-local`

`Adder::bump(inout $n)` binds a local, and `Adder::bump(inout $obj->n)` binds an instance property whose
class is known while compiling. Those are the two places `nvs-ir`'s `write_back_ref` can stage a reference
to. `bump(inout $a["k"])`, a static property, a property with hooks, a property named by a key, a call's
result and a literal are refused at the call with `E0439`, and that is the rule rather than a gap.

The mechanism is copy-in/copy-back through a cell the call stages, and an element has no cell of its own to
stage. The write-back would have to re-run the whole access path after the callee returns, against an array
that may have been reallocated meanwhile. A hooked property would run its hook a second time.

The rewrite is the mechanism written out — read into a local, pass the local, store it back — and it is
what the diagnostic's help says.

<sub>See also [`statements/inout-is-written-at-the-call`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-written-at-the-call), [`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling).</sub>

<a id="statements-there-is-no-out-mode"></a>

## There is no write-only `out` mode

`rule:statements/there-is-no-out-mode`

`inout` invites the question of a write-only `out` mode: assigned before return, unreadable on entry. There
is none.

It is a separate feature needing its own definite-assignment analysis pointed at parameters rather than at
properties, and nothing asks for it. This is recorded so it is not reopened as a corollary of the `inout`
spelling.

<sub>See also [`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling).</sub>

<a id="statements-ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker"></a>

## `&` in a by-reference position is refused at parse time

`rule:statements/ampersand-is-not-a-by-reference-marker`

`&` where a by-reference marker would go is still recognised, so the diagnostic can name the exact fix, and
produces an error node — the AST keeps no variant for it. `E0237`: *`&` is not a by-reference marker in
Novis — write `inout` before the type.*

`&` keeps its other three jobs unchanged: `$a & $b` is bitwise AND, `$a && $b` is logical AND, and `A&B` is
an intersection type. Its other two PHP meanings, a by-reference binding and a by-reference return
(`function &bump`), are both `E0237`. With them gone, an `&` in a type position always means an
intersection. The one-token lookahead that told `int &$x` apart from an intersection continuation
survives the removal of the meaning it was written for, because meaning it and parsing it are two different
questions: the type parser reaches that `&` first, and consuming it as an intersection member would leave
the site above it nothing to report but a malformed intersection.

The already-refused spellings keep their own codes and gain the new word in their help text: `$a = &$b` is
`E0701`, an anonymous function parameter `E0493`, a generator's `E0492`.

<sub>See also [`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling), [`statements/inout-is-written-at-the-call`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-written-at-the-call).</sub>

<a id="statements-exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword"></a>

## `exit` is the only process-termination keyword; `die` is refused

`rule:statements/exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword`

`exit` is the only process-termination keyword. `die`, `die()` and `die('bye')` are still recognised — with
the optional `(status)`/`(message)` argument parsed identically — solely so the diagnostic can point at the
fix, and they produce an error node rather than an exit node: *use `exit` instead — it is the only
process-termination keyword Novis keeps.* The code is `E0228`.

The pair had no behavioural difference to preserve: both parsed to one shape with one argument, and both
were type-checked and lowered identically. Of ten other languages with a termination primitive, every one
keeps at most one plain spelling of it; where a second primitive exists it is a genuinely different
behaviour — skips cleanup, cannot be caught, crashes instead of exiting — never a bare synonym. PHP's
`die` is itself a borrowed name without its meaning: Perl's `die` raises a catchable error distinct from
Perl's `exit`, and PHP kept the word but made it a plain duplicate. A second spelling of one construct is
what [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) rules out, and rewriting `die(...)` to `exit(...)` is
a rename with the argument unchanged.

**Declined:**
- **`die` as a permanent alias of `exit`.** It differs in nothing, so it buys only a second thing to
  teach.
- **`die` as a second tier, the way Ruby has `exit!` or Python `os._exit`.** No such distinction exists
  in the request or process model to hang a second keyword on, and inventing one only to keep two
  spellings solves nothing.
- **Dropping only one of `die` and `<?php`.** Both are duplicate spellings with no behavioural
  difference ([`statements/nvs-is-the-only-open-tag`](statements.md#statements-nvs-is-the-only-open-tag)), so keeping one would need a reason neither has.

<sub>See also [`statements/nvs-is-the-only-open-tag`](statements.md#statements-nvs-is-the-only-open-tag), [`statements/exit-stops-the-program-where-it-stands`](statements.md#statements-exit-stops-the-program-where-it-stands).</sub>

<a id="statements-exit-stops-the-program-where-it-stands"></a>

## `exit` ends the program where it stands: no `catch` sees it, no `finally` runs, and a clean exit is not a failure

`rule:statements/exit-stops-the-program-where-it-stands`

`exit` and `exit(n)` end the program from any frame. No `catch` sees the ending, and no `finally`
between the call and the root runs, in the frame that called it or in any frame above. `exit(n)`
ends with status `n`; `exit("message")` writes the message and ends with status `0`. An operand that
is neither an `int` nor a `string` is a type mismatch at the operand, because
[`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion) has no implicit conversion to offer there.

Running no `finally` is PHP's own behaviour for `exit`, checked against PHP's output rather than
assumed, so it is what a program observes and not a simplification. A program that has cleanup to run
on the way out uses `Core\Script::finish()` instead, and one that must act on every ending registers
an exit hook ([`observability/three-endings-fire-the-exit-queue`](observability.md#observability-three-endings-fire-the-exit-queue)).

`exit` is a status of its own on [`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation)'s calling convention, `EXITED`, beside
`OK`, `THROWN` and `FATAL`, and the status `n` it named travels on the request context rather than in
the status word. It shares propagation with `FATAL`: neither is catchable, because a `catch` admits
only `THROWN`, and neither runs a `finally`, because every `finally` sits behind that same
comparison. It does not share what a `FATAL` means. A `FATAL` is a failure, escalated and reported at
the request boundary as one ([`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder)), while `exit(0)` is the most ordinary
way a program ends, so the boundary reports the status and not an error. The frame's locals are
still released, because `exit` is an ordinary helper call carrying the error edge every call has.

- **Memory:** one 64-bit integer per request, the status `exit` named. Every status check already
  compares against `OK`, so the extra status adds no instruction to a call site.

**Declined:**
- **`exit` as a `FATAL` carrying a code.** Every clean exit would be reported as an internal error,
  and the escalation ladder would run for a program that ended normally.
- **`exit` as a `throw` of a dedicated class.** A `catch (Throwable)` or a `finally` would then
  observe it, which PHP's `exit` never allows.

<sub>See also [`statements/exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword`](statements.md#statements-exit-is-the-only-termination-keyword), [`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation), [`observability/three-endings-fire-the-exit-queue`](observability.md#observability-three-endings-fire-the-exit-queue).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-body-never-falls-off-its-end"></a>

## A non-`void` body hands back a value at every exit; nothing returns `null` for a declaration it did not make

`rule:statements/a-body-never-falls-off-its-end`

A body checked against a declared non-`void` return type never reaches its own end: that path writes
no value at all, and there is no implicit conversion by which `null` becomes the declared type, so
accepting it would change what a binding holds behind its declaration — the one thing the type system
never does. The body is refused where it is written (`E0739`).

A written `return;` is the same promise broken at the other exit, and is refused the same way
(`E0822`). Both are read over every block body checked against a declared type — a method's, a `get`
hook's and a block-bodied `fn`'s alike.

`void`, and a declaration that writes no return type at all (a constructor), promise nothing and are
untouched; so is a generator, whose body [`iteration/generators`](iteration.md#iteration-generators) leaves no return value to
produce. The analysis is asymmetric on purpose, and `nvs_types::returns` owns it: a `while (true)`
with no `break`, a `switch` with a `default`, a `try` every path of which exits, and a body that
always throws are all exits, and every shape it cannot prove reaches the end is treated as one — so
the refusal costs no program that ran. A call to a `never` function, or to a `never` method no
subclass overrides, is an exit too. An overridden one is not, because an override's return type is
not yet checked against the method it replaces. Whether a written `return;` is legal asks none of
that: the declared type is the whole answer.

A `never` body is asked about the falling-off path like any other, and refused (`E0739`) when one
reaches its end. That refusal is also what makes counting a `never` call as an exit sound.

<sub>See also [`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration), [`iteration/generators`](iteration.md#iteration-generators), [`classes/constructor-is-a-method-named-constructor`](classes.md#classes-constructor-is-a-method-named-constructor).</sub>

<a id="statements-continue-always-continues-a-loop"></a>

## `continue` always continues a loop, and a written level counts the way PHP counts

`rule:statements/continue-always-continues-a-loop`

A `switch` owns `break` and nothing else, so `continue` always continues the innermost enclosing loop. A
bare `continue` inside a `switch` moves that loop to its next iteration. PHP counts a `switch` as a
looping structure for `continue`, so a bare one there behaves as `break`, and PHP warns that the
program probably meant `continue 2`. Novis takes the meaning that warning points at.

A written level counts the way PHP counts. `break N` and `continue N` name the `N`-th enclosing
statement, and a `switch` is one of them for both keywords. A level that lands on a `switch` for
`continue` then walks further out to the nearest loop. So `continue 2` inside a `switch` means here
exactly what it means in PHP, and the one divergence stays where the bare keyword put it: a level
naming a `switch` for `continue` continues the loop instead of breaking the `switch`.

A level with nothing to name is `E0475` where it is written, never a panic. That is a level that is not
a literal, a `0`, a level past the enclosing depth, and a `continue` with no loop at or outside its
frame. PHP refuses all four at compile time too, because a level resolves to a statically known
statement and one that names none has nothing to lower to.

**Declined:**
- **A bare `continue` in a `switch` behaving as `break`.** A keyword that means one thing inside a
  `switch` and another everywhere else costs simplicity, and the compatibility it buys is one PHP
  itself warns against.
- **Counting loops alone for a written level.** It would silently retarget `continue 2` inside a
  `switch` inside two nested loops from the inner loop to the outer one, which is worse than a
  diagnostic, and it would make PHP's own `continue 2` inside a `switch` in one loop name a loop that
  is not there.

<sub>See also [`expressions/switch-match-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-switch-match-equality).</sub>

<a id="statements-a-try-has-a-clause-and-a-catch-names-one-class"></a>

## A `try` has a `catch` or a `finally`, and a `catch` clause names exactly one class

`rule:statements/a-try-has-a-clause-and-a-catch-names-one-class`

A `try` has at least one `catch` clause or a `finally`, and a `catch` clause names exactly one class.
A bare `try { … }` guards nothing and is the shape a deleted clause leaves behind: it is `E0242`. PHP
refuses it too.

`catch (A | B $e)` is `E0245`. The binding carries one static type ([`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration)'s `catch`
position), and a clause naming two classes has no single type to give it. A body shared by two classes
is written as two clauses, or as one clause naming a class they both extend. That is the shape
[`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression) already requires of an expression arm, and the two refusals use
the same words.

Both are parse-time refusals in the rejected-PHP band, and each diagnostic names its rewrite.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration).</sub>

<a id="statements-no-return-leaves-a-finally"></a>

## A `return` never leaves a `finally` block, and neither does a `break` or `continue` whose target lies outside it

`rule:statements/no-return-leaves-a-finally`

`return` inside `finally` does not compile. It would replace whatever the region was leaving with —
including a throw in flight, which would be discarded with no `catch` anywhere in the program, the
one way an exception could vanish without a handler. The diagnostic names the two rewrites: change
the result in a `catch`, or after the region.

`break` and `continue` whose target lies outside the `finally` are refused on the same grounds; a
loop wholly inside the block keeps both.

`yield` inside `finally` does not compile either (`E0255`). The block also runs with a throw in
flight and while an abandoned generator unwinds ([`iteration/generators`](iteration.md#iteration-generators)), and neither path can
suspend. PHP allows it.

**An error that leaves a `finally` keeps the one in flight.** A `throw` in the block, or a call in it
that throws, is not refused: the error it raises gets the error in flight as its `previous` when its
own `previous` is `null`. When its `previous` is already set, it leaves unchanged and the error in
flight is dropped, because one error has one `previous` and the program set it. A `try` written
inside the block catches first, so an error it handles changes nothing. A `finally` that completes
re-raises the error in flight unchanged.

Whether an override was a bug (usually) or intent is the author's call, so the diagnostic names both
rewrites and picks neither.

**Memory:** none. The checks run in the front end, and the chaining reuses the `previous` slot every
error already has.

**Latency:** one field read and one null test, only on a throw out of a `finally`.

**Declined:**
- **A run-time deprecation warning, with the spelling still allowed.** The line can be refused where it
  is written, and a warning would only permit for a while code that is refused afterwards
  ([`expressions/no-keyword-logical-operators`](expressions.md#expressions-no-keyword-logical-operators)).
- **Refusing a `throw` in a `finally`.** A direct `throw` could be refused where it is written, but a
  call in the block can throw too, and refusing every call there would leave a `finally` that cannot
  close a file. Chaining covers both with one behaviour.
- **Appending the error in flight to the end of the new error's chain.** It would keep both when
  `previous` is set, but it writes into an error the program built and may still hold elsewhere.

<sub>See also [`statements/a-body-never-falls-off-its-end`](statements.md#statements-a-body-never-falls-off-its-end).</sub>

<a id="statements-let-and-is-are-reserved"></a>

## `let` and `is` cannot name anything; `var` declares, `as` converts, and `is` is the type test

`rule:statements/let-and-is-are-reserved`

Neither `let` nor `is` may name a class, interface, trait, enum, constant, function or parameter.
Reserving a word costs nothing while no program uses it, and taking one back later is a breaking
rename, so both are reserved now.

**The two are reserved for unrelated reasons, and only one of them still has no construct.**

- **`let` is the empty kind** — the family of `eval`, `goto` and `list`, where the spelling is held
  and nothing is behind it, so nothing a user wrote has to be renamed out from under a future
  decision.
- **`is` is not.** It is the type test, `$x is T` ([`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test)), and the only one there is.
- **`instanceof` is neither**, and is the third spelling this rule's diagnostics have to know about:
  it is a word Novis refuses where it is written, naming `is` as the rewrite
  ([`types/one-type-test`](types.md#types-one-type-test)). It was never a name, so nothing is reserved by refusing it — the token
  exists only so the refusal can spell it.

The diagnostics name the living spellings: `var` declares an inferred local
([`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference)), `is` tests ([`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing)) and `as` converts
([`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion)). Like every reserved word, both match in lower case only
([`classes/reserved-spellings-are-lower-case`](classes.md#classes-reserved-spellings-are-lower-case)).

Either word is `E0247` in three places, all reported by one helper
(`crates/nvs-syntax/src/parser/mod.rs:781`): where an expression starts
(`crates/nvs-syntax/src/parser/expr.rs:1501`); as the name of every declaration — a class,
interface, trait, enum, enum case, constant, method or `type` alias — through `parse_decl_name`
(`crates/nvs-syntax/src/parser/decl.rs:366`); and as a parameter, `$let` or `$is`, a promoted
constructor parameter included, in `parse_param` (`crates/nvs-syntax/src/parser/expr.rs:2048`). The
name is kept after the report, so the parse goes on and nothing else is reported for it. A member
reference after `->` or `::` still admits both words, since it declares nothing and no declaration
can match it. That is how `Core\Router\Match::is` is called: `Core` declares it, which a program
cannot, and the editor's stub of it is the one declaration the parser reports and keeps.

**Declined:**
- **Reserving `is` alone and leaving `let` free.** Reserving the second word costs the same as the
  first, and freeing it again stays possible where taking it back is not.

<sub>See also [`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference), [`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing), [`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test), [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion), [`classes/reserved-spellings-are-lower-case`](classes.md#classes-reserved-spellings-are-lower-case), [`security/no-eval`](security.md#security-no-eval), [`types/one-type-test`](types.md#types-one-type-test).</sub>
